video_title: The Outlook for Data Center Power Demand as AI Token Use Grows
gist: Goldman Sachs analysts Carly Davenport (US utilities) and Brian Singer (GS Sustain), with hosts Allison Nathan and George Lee, raise their power-demand forecasts again — US load to a 3.5% CAGR through 2030, US data center demand to 108GW (from 83GW), and global data center power up ~170% from 2025 to 2030 — because hyperscaler capex forecasts jumped ($1.2T to $1.7T for 2027; $1.5T to $2.1T for 2029) and real efficiency gains are being swamped by token demand. The binding constraint has shifted from megawatts to turbines, transformers, tradespeople, interconnection queues and, above all, public/political pushback: over 300 local moratoria versus one state-level moratorium today, which the panel names as the steepest hill to climb.

insights.claim: Goldman Sachs raised its US power demand forecast to a 3.5% CAGR through 2030 from a prior 3.2% CAGR, with year-to-date US power demand growth already running above 4%.
insights.speaker: Carly Davenport
insights.so_what: A raised and already-outrunning-forecast load curve underpins regulated utility rate-base growth and IPP pricing; watch for further upward revisions as the confirming signal.
insights.quote: we recently raised our forecast up to a 3.5% CAGR through 2030. And that was up from our prior forecast of about 3.2% CAGR through 2030.

insights.claim: US data center power demand in 2030 was revised up to roughly 108 gigawatts from about 83 gigawatts, a ~25% increase, driven by new projects entering the development queue (per 451 Research data).
insights.speaker: Carly Davenport
insights.so_what: A 25GW upward revision in a single forecast cycle sizes the incremental addressable market for turbines, transformers, gas and grid equipment suppliers.

insights.claim: Data center vacancy rates across all major US markets have compressed to roughly 1-2%, down from a 2-7% range in recent years, so the demand upgrade comes from higher utilization of existing capacity as well as new builds.
insights.speaker: Carly Davenport
insights.so_what: Sub-2% vacancy means pricing power for existing data center owners and implies incremental AI load lands on the grid faster than new construction timelines suggest; Goldman still models a 3% US average vacancy rate in 2030.

insights.claim: Goldman's hyperscaler capex projections rose from $1.2 trillion to $1.7 trillion for 2027 and from $1.5 trillion to $2.1 trillion for 2029 in roughly four months (March to August 2026).
insights.speaker: Brian Singer
insights.so_what: The pace of upward capex revision — ~40% in a single quarter of forecasting — is itself the signal; it flows straight through to power, server shipment and equipment forecasts.
insights.quote: we were projecting and our analysts were projecting hyperscaler spending was at about $1.2 trillion for 2027. That's $1.7 trillion now.

insights.claim: Global data center power demand in 2030 is now forecast up about 170% from 2025 levels, versus about 117% growth forecast just months earlier in March.
insights.speaker: Brian Singer
insights.so_what: The global figure is being revised faster than the US figure, arguing for exposure to ex-US grid, gas and equipment supply chains, not just US utilities.

insights.claim: Counting from the start of 2024 through the end of the decade, AI is adding power consumption equivalent to the entire country of Japan, the world's fifth-largest power consumer.
insights.speaker: Brian Singer
insights.so_what: A sovereign-scale framing for sizing the total opportunity across generation, transmission and fuel over a seven-year window.
insights.quote: it's adding the power equivalent of the whole country of Japan, which is the number five power consuming country.

insights.claim: Anticipated AI efficiency gains are genuinely materializing across models, chips and the supply chain, yet demand growth is overwhelming them — making the demand curve steeper than headline numbers alone suggest.
insights.speaker: George Lee
insights.so_what: Efficiency headlines are not a short thesis on power; treat model-efficiency news as demand-expanding rather than demand-destroying until enterprise budgets actually fall.
insights.quote: all those expected or anticipated efficiency gains are actually happening. And yet, the demand profile is both recovering those and expanding at the rate you described.

insights.claim: Cheaper tokens and more judicious token usage widen the horizon of economically addressable enterprise tasks, expanding rather than shrinking the addressable market for compute — a Jevons-style dynamic explicitly described for AI tokens.
insights.speaker: George Lee
insights.so_what: Frame declining cost-per-token as TAM expansion for inference and power, which supports long-duration infrastructure exposure rather than a cyclical peak call.
insights.quote: Tokens get cheaper. You're more efficient with their usage. And that expands the demand or the addressable market for this commodity.

insights.claim: Productivity gains have not yet reduced corporate tech and R&D budgets; the key cycle-turning question is when buyers decide to spend less for the same tokens rather than the same amount for more tokens.
insights.speaker: Brian Singer
insights.so_what: This is the explicit trigger to watch for the AI capex cycle rolling over — budget-level substitution, not model-level efficiency.
insights.quote: when will we get to a point where consumers will see these productivity gains and say, instead of spending the same amount of money and consuming more tokens and compute, I'm going to spend less money and consume the same tokens and compute.

insights.claim: Enterprise customers are beginning to scrutinize how and where they consume tokens to reduce consumption intensity without hurting output, an early sign of demand discipline that has not yet dented aggregate token appetite.
insights.speaker: Brian Singer
insights.so_what: An early-warning indicator: watch for token-optimization behavior to broaden from routing choices into actual budget cuts.

insights.claim: PJM houses about 35% of US data center power demand today and is expected to hold that 35% share through 2030, supported by merchant nuclear capacity, a high-voltage transmission backbone and existing data center clusters.
insights.speaker: Carly Davenport
insights.so_what: PJM-exposed generators and utilities remain the core play on data center load, though the panel also flags PJM as the tightest market and most populous corridor for pushback.

insights.claim: MISO — the mid-continent market from Minnesota to Louisiana — is expected to overtake ERCOT, the Southeast and the Pacific Northwest to become the second-largest US data center market by 2030 at roughly 16% share, a shift the analyst called surprising.
insights.speaker: Carly Davenport
insights.so_what: A non-consensus regional rotation: regulated utilities in Iowa, Wisconsin and Louisiana capture rate-based generation build that would go to merchant developers in PJM or ERCOT.
insights.quote: the MISO market, which is the mid-continent of the US, so think from Minnesota down to Louisiana, is going to overtake ERCOT, the Southeast, and the Northwest and become the second largest data center market in the U.S. by 2030.

insights.claim: ERCOT holds about 15% of US data center demand today and is projected to slip to third at about 14% by 2030, with added uncertainty from the Texas governor's actions auditing data center projects.
insights.speaker: Carly Davenport
insights.so_what: Texas loses relative share despite absolute growth; political audit risk is now a discrete overhang on ERCOT-linked development pipelines.

insights.claim: Regulated utilities win data center business in MISO because they are a one-stop shop — generation, transmission and distribution from a single counterparty with existing regulator and community relationships — versus deregulated markets where a customer must negotiate separately with a developer and the wires utility.
insights.speaker: Carly Davenport
insights.so_what: Explains why capital is rotating toward regulated names: simpler contracting plus regulator-set pricing that manages affordability optics.

insights.claim: Goldman does not forecast a nationwide US power shortage, but sees certain regions becoming critically tight — PJM at the top of that list today, with ERCOT expected to tighten as demand ramps around 2028.
insights.speaker: Carly Davenport
insights.so_what: Scarcity is a regional trade, not a national one; PJM capacity/energy pricing is the near-term expression, ERCOT the 2028 setup.

themes.theme: The seven Ps of supply constraints

insights.claim: Goldman's constraint framework has expanded from six Ps to seven — pervasiveness of AI, productivity, price of power, policy (permitting, pushback, populism), parts, people, and a newly added physical environment — as the binding limits move from megawatts to equipment, labor and siting.
insights.speaker: Brian Singer
insights.so_what: A ready-made checklist for diligencing any data center power investment; the newly added P (physical environment/cooling) is where the market is least positioned.

insights.claim: A major turbine manufacturer said on its most recent conference call that by the end of this year it expects to be half sold out for 2031, showing how far out gas turbine capacity is already committed.
insights.speaker: Brian Singer
insights.so_what: Turbine backlogs stretching to 2031 mean pricing power for OEMs and force near-term power sourcing toward simple-cycle gas, renewables and storage rather than combined cycle.
insights.quote: One of the major turbine manufacturers on their most recent conference call said that they expect that by the end of this year, they'll be halfway sold out for 2031.

insights.claim: Equipment scarcity constrains how power is sourced rather than total power demand, producing a sequencing of natural gas simple cycle plus renewables and battery storage near term, combined cycle gas in the medium term, and nuclear in the long term.
insights.speaker: Brian Singer
insights.so_what: A dated roadmap for rotating across generation technologies rather than betting on one; near-term winners are simple-cycle gas and storage, not nuclear.

insights.claim: Skilled trades are a hard constraint because a decade of flat US power demand gave little incentive to enter fields like high-voltage electrical work and welding, and certification takes at least four years of training.
insights.speaker: Brian Singer
insights.so_what: Labor supply cannot respond inside the current build cycle, supporting persistent cost inflation for engineering and construction and favoring firms with captive craft labor.

insights.claim: More than half of data centers are being built in areas with elevated physical risk — extreme temperatures, humidity or drought — which forces an explicit cooling trade-off between consuming more water and less power or more power and less water.
insights.speaker: Brian Singer
insights.so_what: Siting-driven cooling choices are an underappreciated swing factor in per-site power intensity; watch cooling technology vendors and water-constrained regions like West Texas.
insights.quote: More than half of them are built in areas with elevated physical risk, either extreme temperatures, humidity, drought.

insights.claim: In the US the priority will be minimizing water use — because new water sources are far more expensive to find than new power sources — which means deploying cooling technologies that raise power usage effectiveness, whereas China's regulations push the opposite way toward minimizing power consumption.
insights.speaker: Brian Singer
insights.so_what: US water-first policy mechanically adds to US power demand forecasts; the divergent China stance means US and Chinese data centers should not be modeled with the same power intensity.
insights.quote: It's a lot more expensive to find new sources of water than it is to find new sources of power.

insights.claim: Goldman raised its behind-the-meter estimate to about 30 gigawatts of on-site gas capacity by 2030, delivering just over 20 gigawatts of power and accounting for roughly 20% of its 2030 data center demand estimate.
insights.speaker: Carly Davenport
insights.so_what: A fifth of forecast data center load bypasses the grid entirely, sizing a distinct market for on-site gen sets, reciprocating engines and aeroderivative turbines separate from utility rate base.

insights.claim: Behind-the-meter islanded power is a bridge solution rather than a permanent one, because the largest data center customers repeatedly say they prefer grid connection — the grid is more cost-effective and more reliable, and multi-gigawatt campuses need it over time.
insights.speaker: Carly Davenport
insights.so_what: Off-grid capacity built today may eventually reconnect and become grid resource, so behind-the-meter demand is a queue-driven, time-limited opportunity rather than a structural displacement of utilities.
insights.quote: behind the meter is more of a bridge solution and it is not a long-term solution.

insights.claim: Some data center projects are being structured with the flexibility to start behind the meter if a grid connection is unavailable for a 2028 in-service date and then transition onto the grid later.
insights.speaker: Carly Davenport
insights.so_what: Dual-path project design de-risks development timelines and favors suppliers who can serve both islanded and interconnected configurations.

insights.claim: Regulatory uncertainty over how data center connections will be handled is the single most important issue facing power and utilities companies today, with interconnection queues running two, three, five or even seven years depending on the regional grid.
insights.speaker: Carly Davenport
insights.so_what: Queue length is the mechanism converting AI demand into behind-the-meter and special-tariff workarounds; regulatory clarity would be a re-rating catalyst for utilities.
insights.quote: the regulatory uncertainty on how data center connections will be handled is probably the single most important issue facing power and utilities companies today.

insights.claim: Regulated markets are pushing toward standardized, transparent special tariff structures pre-approved by regulators — covering timelines, financial requirements and customer protections — to streamline data center connections without shifting reliability or affordability risk onto other ratepayers.
insights.speaker: Carly Davenport
insights.so_what: Approved large-load tariffs plus take-or-pay commitments are the practical gate on how fast regulated utilities can monetize data center demand; track approvals state by state.

insights.claim: Utilities are proactively quantifying customer bill savings and in some cases agreeing not to raise rates for a period of time as a way to make data center growth politically survivable.
insights.speaker: Carly Davenport
insights.so_what: Rate freezes traded for load growth cap near-term regulated revenue upside but reduce the risk of adverse political intervention — a trade-off to test in utility earnings models.

insights.claim: There is currently one state-level data center moratorium in the US but more than 300 regional or local moratoria across the country, a base that could grow and inhibit buildout absent better industry messaging.
insights.speaker: George Lee
insights.so_what: The single most concrete, countable leading indicator in the episode: moratorium counts escalating from local to state level would mark the constraint side winning.
insights.quote: there's a single state-level data center moratorium today. But there are more than 300 regional or local moratoria going on around the country.

insights.claim: Popular sentiment, not physics or supply chains, may be the steepest hill to climb in balancing power supply and demand — an analogy drawn to how populist and political opposition halted the US nuclear industry in the 1970s.
insights.speaker: George Lee
insights.so_what: Underwrite political risk, not just engineering risk, in long-dated data center and generation projects; the historical precedent is an industry that was stopped outright.
insights.quote: this dimension of popular sentiment might be the steepest hill we have to climb in getting to the right balance of supply and demand here.

insights.claim: A survey cited on the program found that a plurality of Americans would rather have a nuclear power plant in their neighborhood than a data center, indicating data centers have inherited AI's reputational baggage.
insights.speaker: George Lee
insights.so_what: A striking measure of siting risk: community opposition to data centers may exceed opposition to the technology historically considered least welcome.
insights.quote: I read a survey recently that said that a plurality of Americans would prefer to have a nuclear power plant in their neighborhood versus a data center.

insights.claim: Community pushback breaks into five concerns — outage risk, power price surges, water use, noise, and waste heat raising local temperatures — each with an existing technical mitigant: interruptibility agreements, take-or-pay contracts, closed-loop or dry cooling, noise abatement, and waste heat capture as practiced in Finland.
insights.speaker: Brian Singer
insights.so_what: Maps each opposition argument to a purchasable technology or contract structure, identifying vendor categories that benefit as social license becomes a build requirement.

insights.claim: Interruptibility — data centers agreeing to be curtailed or disconnected when the grid faces an outage — is becoming a license to operate, with some governments putting such requirements in place.
insights.speaker: Brian Singer
insights.so_what: Curtailable load changes the economics of AI training siting and creates value for on-site backup and flexible-load management providers.
insights.quote: It's becoming license to operate for the data centers to be willing to be disconnected or to be cut off in the event, the grid is about to undergo an outage.

insights.claim: Hyperscaler customers have little appetite to force projects into hostile communities while other communities actively court data centers for tax base, construction jobs and local infrastructure investment, which is likely to increase geographic concentration of data centers.
insights.speaker: Carly Davenport
insights.so_what: Expect load and associated utility capex to cluster further into welcoming jurisdictions — a concentration effect that sharpens the regional utility trade.
insights.quote: those communities want it until they get it. And then they are living through these issues and problems.

themes.theme: Utility funding and signposts to watch

insights.claim: Capital investment across Goldman's regulated utilities coverage is set to rise about 60% over the next five years versus the prior five-year period, yet leverage still sits roughly 100 basis points of cushion above credit downgrade thresholds because companies have proactively issued equity.
insights.speaker: Carly Davenport
insights.so_what: Balance sheets can fund the build, but persistent equity issuance is a structural dilution headwind for regulated utility shareholders.

insights.claim: Goldman expects incremental utility capital to be funded roughly 30% to 50% with equity.
insights.speaker: Carly Davenport
insights.so_what: A concrete equity-supply estimate for the utility sector — sizeable secondary issuance to absorb, and a reason EPS growth may lag rate-base growth.

insights.claim: About 60% of data center power demand is expected to be met with natural gas and 40% with renewables, with a few one-off nuclear plant restarts helping to bridge the gap.
insights.speaker: Carly Davenport
insights.so_what: A concrete fuel-mix split for sizing gas demand and renewables buildout tied to AI load; nuclear restarts are marginal, not central, this decade.

insights.claim: The primary signpost to watch is how many state-level data center moratoriums emerge — as distinct from local ones — particularly heading into the November elections and any resulting policy changeover.
insights.speaker: Carly Davenport
insights.so_what: A specific, dated catalyst window: state-level moratoria post-November would materially raise project delay risk for developers.

insights.claim: Whether the 2030 data center capacity forecast gets revised up or down from here is the core test of the 'field of dreams' assumption that if data centers are built, demand will come.
insights.speaker: Brian Singer
insights.so_what: Direction of forecast revisions, not their level, is the tradeable signal for power and equipment names levered to the buildout.
insights.quote: does this 2030 data center capacity get revised up or down from here? Call it the field of dreams data centers. The "if you build them, they will come."

insights.claim: Nuclear contracting by hyperscalers is an off-the-beaten-path indicator worth tracking precisely because it has almost no effect over the next five years, making it a clean read on their long-term demand conviction and their carbon mitigation stance.
insights.speaker: Brian Singer
insights.so_what: Hyperscaler nuclear PPAs function as a forward signal on post-2030 AI demand belief; new contracts should be read as long-duration conviction, not near-term supply.
insights.quote: if I'm looking for an off the beaten path metric to watch, it would be nuclear contracting by hyperscalers. Only because that's going to have very little effect over the next five years.
